about.addr: Your address. On the same network, devices use a throwaway name and your real address is never looked up. Further away, everything goes through the encrypted connection, so the other device learns nothing about where you are. The site you connect to still sees your address, like any website does.
about.meets: What is still visible. The server that introduces two devices can see that they met, and roughly when. It never sees who you are, or what you sent. Hiding that too takes Tor, and this works there.
about.p1: The code is the password. Both devices turn it into the same key without ever sending it. Nothing in the middle can work the key out, and it gets one guess at the code.
about.p2: Everything is locked before it leaves. File names and sizes too, and each one is padded so nothing in the middle can guess how long it was.
about.p3: Safety words. Both devices work out the same four words from the connection itself. If someone’s in the middle, the two lists won’t match.
about.p4: Files go straight to disk. Nothing piles up in memory, so a huge file needs no more room than a small one.
about.p5: Paired devices stay anonymous. They meet under a name that changes every ten minutes, so nothing in the middle ever sees the same one twice.
about.p6: One thing to know. This is a web page, so every time you open it you’re trusting the code it sends you. That is the one thing no design here can remove.
about.pq: Built for later, too. The key is agreed in two separate ways at once, and you’d have to break both. One of them is designed to hold up against quantum computers, so a recording saved today stays shut.
about.tag: Nothing in the middle can read your files, pretend to be one of your devices, or recognise you from one visit to the next.

net.p1: How it works. The encrypted connection gives your network a label and hands the same one to every device connecting from there. Devices with this on use it to find each other.
net.p2: What it costs. For six hours at a time, the encrypted connection can tell that two devices are on the same network. It still can’t see your files, their names or their sizes.
net.p3: Still check. A device found this way stays unverified until you confirm the safety words.
net.statusOn: Devices on this network can find you
net.unavailable: The encrypted connection didn’t offer a network label
relay.p1: It can’t read a file, a name or a message. Those stay locked the whole way.
relay.p2: It can see which devices you meet and when, and it could try to sit in the middle. That’s what the safety words catch.
relay.p3: Not expecting this? Keep yours. A link that quietly swaps your encrypted connection is how someone would watch who you talk to.
relay.sub: The encrypted connection is what introduces your devices to each other. It never sees your files, only who you meet and when.
relay.title: This link wants to change your encrypted connection
risk.note: This kind of file opens by running. Take it only from someone you know, and only if you expected it.
